description: Test your knowledge of PA G7 | Diagnostic Cytology & Clinical Pathology.

cards.text: What is the fundamental difference between cytology and histopathology?
cards.answer: Cytology examines individual cells or cell clusters on smears without tissue architecture, while histopathology examines intact tissue sections preserving spatial relationships and stromal reaction.

tip.tip: Cyto = cells alone; Histo = cells + structure

cards.text: What is the main limitation of cytology in tumor diagnosis?
cards.answer: Cytology cannot determine invasion depth, assess stromal reaction, or identify architectural patterns needed to classify certain tumors (e.g., follicular adenoma vs carcinoma of thyroid).

cards.text: Why is the cervical transformation zone (TZ) specifically sampled in a Pap smear?
cards.answer: The TZ is the junction between the squamocolumnar junction of the ectocervix and endocervix where squamous metaplasia and carcinogenesis begin—the site of precancerous changes.

cards.text: What does HSIL stand for in the Bethesda System, and what does it represent?
cards.answer: HSIL = High-Grade Squamous Intraepithelial Lesion, representing CIN 2/3 (cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grades 2-3), requiring immediate evaluation and management.

cards.text: What percentage of cervical squamous cell carcinomas are caused by persistent high-risk HPV infection?
cards.answer: More than 95% of cervical squamous cell carcinomas are caused by persistent infection with high-risk HPV types, particularly HPV-16 and HPV-18.

cards.text: Name two key advantages of cytology as a screening tool compared to histopathology.
cards.answer: Cytology is rapid (hours vs 1-3 days), minimally invasive (no operating theatre required), cheaper, highly acceptable to patients, and allows serial monitoring and repeat sampling.

cards.text: What are koilocytes and what intraepithelial lesion do they indicate on Pap smear?
cards.answer: Koilocytes are squamous cells with a characteristic perinuclear halo and irregular nuclear membranes, indicative of HPV effect seen in LSIL (Low-Grade Squamous Intraepithelial Lesion).

cards.text: What is the major clinical consequence when a negative cytology report is obtained in a clinically suspicious case?
cards.answer: A negative (normal) cytology report is NOT definitively reassuring and does not exclude malignancy; histological biopsy may still be required if clinical suspicion remains high due to sampling error limitations.
